title: Practice: how greedy, ε-greedy and UCB choose
note: Four problems in 17 minutes (2026-11-16: P8 added, the time raised from 12): P7 (greedy after a lucky start: the favourite's average falls with a poor day and greedy switches; needs greedy's own rule, n05.f1, which no problem needed before, so a learner who taught "greedy sticks with the trial winner" sees Kai go wrong; 2026-11-05, after two pilot sessions where both learners missed the test's lucky-start greedy items, T1 and V11), P3 (greedy against UCB after an unlucky start), P2 (what one pick does to every score) and P8 (UCB over a long run: the least-liked playlist came back about once every 100 hours around hour 1,000, and far less often around hour 50,000, since an unpicked bonus keeps growing, but ever more slowly). P8 is the first problem that needs the slowing, the half of n12.f2 that P2 and P3 accept without (their vague reading still leads to the key): Kai's vague reading (a steady rate, so the same pace as before) leads to a wrong option here. It asks V4's idea in one concrete case rather than in general, so a correction has to find the rule behind a specific wrong prediction; V4 left the final test the same day for V21, which asks it in another form (logs to read, with greedy's to tell apart). Without UCB's rule Kai goes for the option tried the fewest times, which is Jazz, so it predicts more plays, not fewer. P8's numbers are the lesson's formula (average + √(ln t / n)) simulated: four playlists averaging 0.7, 0.6, 0.5 and 0.3, scores spread with sd 0.25 and kept between 0 and 1, 40 runs: around hour 1,000 the worst one came back every 89 hours on average (single runs 39 to 153), around hour 50,000 every 4,700 hours (2,100 to 9,100), and it was still played after hour 40,000 in every run (tests/practice.test.ts recomputes them). P7, P3 and P2 each have a caveat, a nuance learners rarely put into words: when Kai would otherwise solve this problem and every one after it, it reads the first one its notes leave open the plausible wrong way (never against the notes); P7's come into play whenever Kai could solve P7 (`alone`). P8's (`slowing`, `always`, 2026-11-16) is the gate's backstop rather than a planted slip: the judge may credit the bonus's growth without the slowing its key asks for (a team test: "the exploration bonus grows when an option is not being picked" as correct), so whenever P8's gate is open and no note on UCB or the bonus says the growth slows, Kai reads the growth as steady (option A), whatever came before, and on the retry while the correction still leaves it open. P3's and P2's wait for P8 to be solvable (its gate open and the slowing said), so they come into play only when the slowing was taught; without it Kai fails P8 instead. On the retry after a correction, the misreading of Kai's first try stays in play while the corrected notes leave its point open (before 2026-11-16 any correction, even "sdas", set Kai right). P4 (audio tours) and the ε-greedy problems are in stash/practice.json. The team's item design (P1 to P6, 2026-11-02) had two rounds of three problems: round 2 repeated round 1's facts in new settings (P4 repeated P2's, P5 P1's and added UCB, P6 P3's over many rounds), so a correction in round 1 could carry over. Options state only the prediction. Answers and worked solutions stay on the server and are shown on the results page after the final test. Each solution step lists the facts it relies on. `needs` lists the teachable facts without which the answer can't be reached, in the order the steps use them: in the recursive condition Kai can only be right when its notebook holds all of them, correctly explained. Given facts (the setup, averages, trying each option once) are never needed: Kai knows them and the stems repeat them. `beliefs` give, for each needed fact, the answer Kai's assumption for that fact leads to (the fact's `assume` in the graph, word for word; `when: vague` for how Kai reads a vague explanation, where that differs). When needed facts are missing, Kai reasons from the assumption of the first one in `needs` order whose assumption leads somewhere wrong, says that it is guessing, and its wrong answer follows from its own steps. Every wrong option is the prediction of a named misconception (Kai's or a known learner one), so no option can be ruled out without the facts.

beliefs.belief: Greedy settles on whichever option leads after the first tries and sticks with it for good, without ever switching.

items.title: Ice-cream flavours
items.prompt: A café features one of three ice-cream flavours each day, chosen with greedy, and scores each day's sales out of 10. The true averages, unknown to the café, are A 8, B 6 and C 5, and most days score within 1 point of their flavour's true average. On the three trial days A scores 7.5, B has an unusually good day and scores 9, and C scores 5. On day 4 greedy features B, which scores 5. Which flavour does greedy feature on day 5, and on most days after that?
options: B on day 5 and after: it won the trials
A on day 5, and mostly A after that
A on day 5, then back to B
C, the one with the least promising start

steps.text: Greedy features the flavour with the highest average so far, and updates the average of the one it features.
After day 4, B's average is (9 + 5) / 2 = 7, below A's 7.5, so on day 5 greedy switches to A.
A's days score around 8, so A's average stays above B's 7, which no longer changes because B isn't featured: mostly A after that.

caveat.about: Greedy compares the averages anew every day, so its favourite can change: when the favourite's average falls below another flavour's, greedy switches to that one. Leading after the trials doesn't make a flavour the favourite for good.
caveat.misreading: B won the trials, so B is greedy's favourite, and greedy sticks with its favourite: A and C fell behind in the trials, so greedy doesn't go back to them. One weaker day for B doesn't change that.

caveat.about: What tells lock-in apart from switching: only a featured flavour's average moves, towards that flavour's true average, while one that isn't featured keeps its average. So lock-in needs an average stuck below the other flavours' true averages. Here B's lucky start keeps falling towards B's true 6, below A's 7.5, so greedy switches to A, and A, now featured, stays ahead around its true 8.

A started worse than B, so I take it this is lock-in for A: greedy doesn't go back to A and keeps featuring B.

items.title: Two cakes
items.prompt: Two cafés test the same two new cakes and score each day's sales out of 10. Cake A is truly better: its days usually score between 7 and 9. Cake B's days always score between 5 and 7. On the first two days both cafés try each cake once; in both, A has an unusually bad day (3) and B scores 6. From then on café 1 uses greedy and café 2 uses UCB. Which café ends up selling mostly cake A?

steps.text: After the first two days, A's average is 3 and B's is 6.
Greedy picks B. B's days score 5 to 7, so B's average stays above 3, greedy never picks A again, and A's average stays at 3.
UCB adds a bonus. Each day B is picked, B's bonus shrinks.
Each day A is not picked, A's bonus grows.
So A's score eventually passes B's, UCB tries A again, A's average rises towards 8, and UCB then mostly sells A.

beliefs.belief: If greedy keeps going, the averages correct themselves over time, so greedy finds the best option in the end.
Every bonus shrinks as rounds pass, whether its option is picked or not.
An option's bonus stays the same while it is not picked.
The bonus of an option that is not picked grows at a steady rate, so a neglected option comes back at regular intervals.
UCB picks the option it is least sure about, the one tried the fewest times, whatever its average.

caveat.about: Cake B's days never score below 5, so its average can never fall to A's 3: once A is behind, greedy never picks it again.
caveat.misreading: Sooner or later B will have a run of bad days that pulls its average below A's 3, and then greedy goes back to A and finds out A is better, so café 1 ends up mostly on A too.

items.title: Exercise types
items.prompt: A language app picks the next exercise type with UCB. Before this round: Flashcards average 6.3, bonus 1.0 (tried 20 times); Dialogues average 5.0, bonus 2.5 (tried 3 times); Listening average 4.0, bonus 1.5 (tried 8 times). UCB picks Dialogues, and the learner scores exactly 5.0 on it. What happens to the three scores (average plus bonus) for the next round?
options: Dialogues' score falls; the other two rise slightly
Dialogues' score falls; the other two stay the same
All three scores stay the same

steps.text: The scores were Flashcards 7.3, Dialogues 7.5 and Listening 5.5, so UCB picked Dialogues.
The new result equals Dialogues' average, so the average stays 5.0.
Dialogues was tried once more, so its bonus shrinks and its score falls.
Flashcards and Listening were not picked, so their bonuses grow slightly with the round number.

beliefs.belief: Every bonus shrinks as rounds pass, whether its option is picked or not.
An option's bonus stays the same while it is not picked.
The bonus of an option that is not picked grows at a steady rate, so a neglected option comes back at regular intervals.

caveat.about: Every round that passes makes the bonus of each option that isn't picked grow a little, even after a single round.
caveat.misreading: My notes say a bonus grows when its option isn't picked for a long time; Flashcards and Listening were only left out for this one round, which isn't long, so their bonuses stay as they were.

caveat.about: A bonus grows with the round number more and more slowly (like ln of the hour), so the longer the app runs, the longer a playlist that isn't played takes to catch up again: the gaps between Jazz's plays keep getting longer.
caveat.misreading: My notes say a playlist's bonus grows while it isn't played. I take that as growing at a steady pace: after each play Jazz's score catches up again in about the same time as before, so UCB keeps coming back to Jazz about once every 100 hours.

items.title: Radio playlists
items.prompt: A radio app picks one of four playlists for each hour with UCB, and scores each hour between 0 and 1 by how many listeners stay tuned. One playlist, Jazz, is clearly the least liked, and by hour 1,000 the app's averages show this. Around hour 1,000, UCB played Jazz about once every 100 hours. The app keeps running for years. How often does UCB play Jazz around hour 50,000?
options: About once every 100 hours, as around hour 1,000
It no longer plays Jazz at all
Far less often than once every 100 hours
More often than once every 100 hours

steps.text: UCB plays the playlist with the highest score, its average plus its bonus.
Each hour Jazz is played, its bonus shrinks, and its score falls back below the best playlist's.
While Jazz isn't played, its bonus keeps growing, so its score always catches up again: around hour 50,000 UCB still plays Jazz.
The bonus grows ever more slowly, so around hour 50,000 it takes far longer to catch up than around hour 1,000: Jazz is played far less often than once every 100 hours.

beliefs.belief: UCB picks the option it is least sure about, the one tried the fewest times, whatever its average.
Every bonus shrinks as rounds pass, whether its option is picked or not.
An option's bonus stays the same while it is not picked.
The bonus of an option that is not picked grows at a steady rate, so a neglected option comes back at regular intervals.
